subject: anatomy
topic: Upper-limb functional design and regional orientation
prompt: Which joint is the only direct bony articulation of the upper limb with the axial skeleton?
explanation: The sternoclavicular joint connects the clavicle to the manubrium and is the upper limb's only direct bony articulation with the axial skeleton.

distractorExplanations.B: The acromioclavicular joint links clavicle to scapula, both components of the upper-limb girdle, rather than directly to the axial skeleton.
distractorExplanations.C: The glenohumeral joint links humerus to scapula and therefore is not the girdle's direct axial articulation.
distractorExplanations.D: The scapulothoracic interface is a functional muscular plane, not a direct synovial bony articulation.

learningObjective: Identify the sternoclavicular joint as the upper limb's only direct bony articulation with the axial skeleton.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed pp. 685-686; local PDF pp. 697-698
source.excerpt: The upper limb is attached to the trunk through the sternoclavicular articulation; the scapulothoracic interface is functional rather than a synovial joint.

subject: anatomy
topic: Upper-limb surface anatomy and integrated clinical localization
prompt: Which movement most directly screens deep ulnar motor function in the hand?
explanation: Resisted finger abduction tests the dorsal interossei, which are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

distractorExplanations.A: Elbow flexion mainly tests musculocutaneous-nerve muscles rather than deep ulnar hand function.
distractorExplanations.C: Thumb interphalangeal extension is produced by extensor pollicis longus through the posterior interosseous/radial pathway.
distractorExplanations.D: Forearm pronation mainly tests median-nerve-supplied pronators rather than the deep ulnar branch.

learningObjective: Select resisted finger abduction as a motor test of the deep ulnar nerve in the hand.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed pp. 827-828; local PDF pp. 839-840
source.excerpt: Finger abduction and adduction provide an anatomical motor test of ulnar-nerve function in the hand.

subject: anatomy
topic: Lower-limb surface anatomy and integrated clinical localization
prompt: At which surface landmark is the dorsalis pedis pulse palpated?

options.text: Immediately lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
Immediately medial to the tibialis anterior tendon

acceptedFreeText: Immediately lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
explanation: Dorsalis pedis is palpated on the dorsum of the foot immediately lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

distractorExplanations.B: Tibialis anterior is more medial; the dorsalis pedis landmark is referenced to extensor hallucis longus.
distractorExplanations.C: The posterior tibial artery, not dorsalis pedis, is palpated posterior to the medial malleolus.
distractorExplanations.D: The small saphenous vein passes behind the lateral malleolus; this is not the dorsalis pedis pulse site.

learningObjective: Locate the dorsalis pedis pulse relative to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed p. 670; local PDF p. 682
source.excerpt: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot immediately lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which term denotes a broad depression on a bone?
explanation: A fossa is a depression in a bone; unlike a groove, it need not be an elongated channel for a passing structure.

distractorExplanations.A: A tubercle is a rounded projection, usually serving as an attachment site.
distractorExplanations.B: A foramen is an opening through a bone for passage of a structure.
distractorExplanations.C: A crest is a prominent linear elevation rather than a depression.

learningObjective: Recognize a fossa as a depression in osteological terminology.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which ligament is the principal vertical stabilizer of the acromioclavicular region?
explanation: The conoid and trapezoid parts of the coracoclavicular ligament suspend the scapula and upper limb from the clavicle and provide the principal vertical stability of the acromioclavicular region.

distractorExplanations.B: The coracoacromial ligament forms an arch over the humeral head and is not the main clavicle-to-scapula suspensory restraint.
distractorExplanations.C: The transverse humeral ligament spans the intertubercular groove and retains the long-head biceps tendon.
distractorExplanations.D: The superior glenohumeral ligament reinforces the shoulder capsule rather than stabilizing the acromioclavicular region vertically.

learningObjective: Identify the coracoclavicular ligament as the principal vertical stabilizer of the acromioclavicular region.

subject: anatomy
topic: Lower-limb function, organization and key pathways
prompt: Which bone transmits most body weight from knee to ankle?
explanation: The tibia is the weight-bearing bone of the leg and transmits most of the load from the knee to the ankle; the fibula chiefly provides attachment and lateral stability.

distractorExplanations.A: The fibula mainly provides muscle attachment and lateral ankle stability and carries little axial load from the knee.
distractorExplanations.C: The patella is a sesamoid within the extensor mechanism and does not transmit axial weight to the ankle.
distractorExplanations.D: The talus receives tibial load at the ankle but does not span the leg from knee to ankle.

learningObjective: Identify the tibia as the principal weight-bearing bone between the knee and ankle.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed pp. 618-619; local PDF pp. 630-631
source.excerpt: The tibia is the major weight-bearing bone of the leg, whereas the fibula carries little axial load.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which distal joint is a fibrous syndesmosis essential to ankle-mortise stability?
explanation: The distal tibiofibular joint is a fibrous syndesmosis whose ligamentous stability maintains the ankle mortise around the talus.

distractorExplanations.A: The proximal tibiofibular joint is a plane synovial joint, not the distal syndesmosis.
distractorExplanations.B: The talonavicular joint is a synovial component of the transverse tarsal complex.
distractorExplanations.D: The subtalar joint is a synovial talocalcaneal articulation for inversion-eversion.

learningObjective: Classify the distal tibiofibular joint as the syndesmosis stabilizing the ankle mortise.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed p. 616; local PDF p. 628
source.excerpt: The distal tibiofibular articulation is a syndesmosis that contributes to ankle-mortise stability.

subject: anatomy
topic: Plantar aponeurosis and fibrous toe sheaths
prompt: Where is the plantar aponeurosis anchored proximally?

options.text: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity

acceptedFreeText: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity
explanation: The thick central plantar aponeurosis is anchored posteriorly to the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity before dividing toward the digits.

distractorExplanations.B: The navicular tuberosity is a tibialis posterior insertion landmark, not the proximal anchor of the plantar aponeurosis.
distractorExplanations.C: The base of the fifth metatarsal receives fibularis brevis and is not the proximal plantar-aponeurosis attachment.
distractorExplanations.D: The sustentaculum tali supports the talus and grooves flexor hallucis longus but is not the aponeurosis origin.

learningObjective: Identify the proximal calcaneal attachment of the plantar aponeurosis.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed p. 649; local PDF p. 661
source.excerpt: The plantar aponeurosis is a thickening of deep fascia anchored to the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which nerve supplies most intrinsic muscles of the sole?
explanation: The lateral plantar nerve supplies most intrinsic muscles of the sole; the medial plantar nerve supplies a smaller group comparable to selected median-nerve targets in the hand.

distractorExplanations.B: Medial plantar nerve supplies a smaller intrinsic group analogous to selected median-nerve targets, not most sole muscles.
distractorExplanations.C: Deep fibular nerve supplies the short extensors on the dorsum and first-web-space skin, not most plantar intrinsic muscles.
distractorExplanations.D: Saphenous nerve is cutaneous in the leg and medial foot and has no intrinsic-foot motor supply.

learningObjective: Identify the lateral plantar nerve as the motor supply to most intrinsic muscles of the sole.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed pp. 659-660; local PDF pp. 671-672
source.excerpt: The lateral plantar nerve supplies most intrinsic muscles in the sole.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which ligament holds the radial head against the radial notch of the ulna?
explanation: The annular ligament attaches to the margins of the radial notch of the ulna and forms a ring that retains the radial head while permitting pronation and supination.

distractorExplanations.A: The ulnar collateral ligament stabilizes the medial elbow against valgus stress rather than encircling the radial head.
distractorExplanations.C: The quadrate ligament reinforces the inferior proximal radioulnar region but is not the principal ring retaining the radial head.
distractorExplanations.D: The interosseous membrane links the forearm shafts and transmits force but does not encircle the radial head.

learningObjective: Identify the annular ligament as the restraint that holds the radial head against the radial notch.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed pp. 774-775; local PDF pp. 786-787
source.excerpt: The annular ligament encircles and retains the radial head at the proximal radioulnar joint.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which bone rotates around the other during pronation?

options.text: Both bones rotate around humerus only

explanation: During pronation the radius rotates and crosses anterior to the relatively stable ulna; in supination the two shafts are parallel.

distractorExplanations.A: The ulna is the relatively stable axis while the radius crosses it in pronation.
distractorExplanations.B: Pronation is produced at proximal and distal radioulnar joints, not solely around the humerus.
distractorExplanations.D: The defining motion of pronation is rotation of the radius around the ulna.

learningObjective: Describe the radius rotating around the ulna during forearm pronation.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed pp. 774-775; local PDF pp. 786-787
source.excerpt: Pronation rotates the radius around the ulna so that their shafts cross.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which radial-nerve-supplied posterior forearm muscle flexes the elbow?
explanation: Brachioradialis is supplied by the radial nerve but crosses anterior to the elbow's flexion-extension axis, so it flexes the elbow most effectively in mid-pronation.

distractorExplanations.A: Extensor carpi radialis longus acts at the wrist, producing extension and radial deviation.
distractorExplanations.B: Supinator rotates the radius into supination and is not a primary elbow flexor.
distractorExplanations.C: Anconeus assists elbow extension and stabilization rather than flexion.

learningObjective: Recognize brachioradialis as the radial-nerve-supplied elbow flexor in the superficial posterior forearm group.

subject: anatomy
prompt: At the radiocarpal joint, which forearm bone directly articulates with scaphoid and lunate?
explanation: The distal radius articulates directly with the scaphoid and lunate; an articular disc separates the ulna from the proximal carpal row.

distractorExplanations.B: An articular disc separates the ulna from the proximal carpal row.
distractorExplanations.C: Capitate is a distal-row carpal participating in midcarpal relations, not a forearm bone in the radiocarpal joint.
distractorExplanations.D: Pisiform is a sesamoid in flexor carpi ulnaris and does not form the radial articular surface.

learningObjective: Identify the radius as the forearm bone directly articulating with the scaphoid and lunate.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed p. 795; local PDF p. 807
source.excerpt: At the wrist, the distal radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate, while the articular disc occupies the ulnar side.

subject: anatomy
topic: Palmar aponeurosis and digital fibrous sheaths
prompt: What is the principal mechanical role of a fibrous digital sheath?
explanation: A fibrous digital sheath holds the flexor tendons close to the phalanges, preventing bowstringing during finger flexion.

distractorExplanations.A: Interphalangeal extension is mediated by the extensor expansion, not by the fibrous flexor sheath.
distractorExplanations.C: The sheath retains flexor tendons; it is not a conduit for an arterial pulse.
distractorExplanations.D: The superficial palmar arch is a vascular anastomosis and is not formed by a digital tendon sheath.

learningObjective: Explain how a fibrous digital sheath prevents flexor-tendon bowstringing.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed p. 801; local PDF p. 813
source.excerpt: Fibrous digital sheaths retain flexor tendons against the phalanges during flexion.

subject: anatomy
prompt: The apex of an extensor hood attaches to which bone?
explanation: The extensor hood's apex attaches to the distal phalanx; its central region separately attaches to the middle phalanx.

distractorExplanations.A: Interossei can insert on the proximal phalanx, but this is not the attachment of the extensor hood's apex.
distractorExplanations.B: The hood's central region attaches to the middle phalanx; the apex continues to the distal phalanx.
distractorExplanations.D: The hood expands over the metacarpophalangeal region but its apex does not attach to the metacarpal head.

learningObjective: Identify the distal-phalanx attachment of the extensor hood apex.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed p. 802; local PDF p. 814
source.excerpt: The apex of the triangular extensor hood attaches to the distal phalanx, and its central region attaches to the middle phalanx.

subject: anatomy
topic: Axillary vein and superficial venous connections
prompt: At which landmark does the axillary vein become the subclavian vein?

options.text: Lateral border of the first rib

acceptedFreeText: Lateral border of the first rib
explanation: The axillary vein crosses the lateral border of the first rib and continues proximally as the subclavian vein.

distractorExplanations.A: At this landmark basilic/brachial veins form the axillary vein; it does not yet become subclavian.
distractorExplanations.B: Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into parts but does not mark the axillary-to-subclavian venous transition.
distractorExplanations.C: The surgical neck is related to axillary nerve and circumflex vessels, not the proximal venous name change.

learningObjective: Locate the axillary-to-subclavian venous transition at the lateral border of the first rib.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.page: Gray's 3e printed pp. 736-738; local PDF pp. 748-750
source.excerpt: The axillary vein becomes the subclavian vein at the lateral border of the first rib.

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which axillary node group receives most lymph from the upper limb?
explanation: Humeral (lateral) axillary nodes receive most lymph from the upper limb; lymph accompanying the cephalic vein may instead reach deltopectoral or apical nodes.

distractorExplanations.B: Pectoral nodes mainly receive anterior thoracic wall and much of the breast.
distractorExplanations.C: Subscapular nodes mainly receive posterior thoracic wall and scapular-region drainage.
distractorExplanations.D: Parasternal nodes lie outside the axillary group and receive drainage along the internal thoracic vessels.

learningObjective: Identify the humeral axillary nodes as the recipients of most upper-limb lymph.
